Name: AS-REP Roasting
Description:
# Description

One or more Active Directory accounts are set to Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication (UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH). With pre-authentication off, any unauthenticated attacker on the network can ask a domain controller for an AS-REP for the account and get back material encrypted with the account's password-derived key. That material cracks offline at GPU speed (hashcat mode 18200). There is no interaction with the account, and nothing the attacker does risks a lockout.

# Impact

An attacker who cracks the AS-REP recovers the account's cleartext password and can then authenticate as that principal. How far that goes depends on the account: a strong, unique password may never crack, while a weak one on a service or legacy admin account (the usual holders of this flag) can hand over privileged access. The request looks like a single Kerberos AS-REQ, not a failed logon, so the capture is quiet on the target.

# Replication Steps
  • List accounts with the flag and request their AS-REPs unauthenticated: GetNPUsers.py {{DOMAIN}}/ -no-pass -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip {{TARGET_HOST}} -format hashcat
  • Crack offline: hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hashes wordlist.txt

Accounts confirmed roastable: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Clear the flag on every affected account: Get-ADUser -Filter 'DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true' | Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false. Put a strong, unique password on the accounts above, and move service identities to (group) Managed Service Accounts, which rotate a 120-character password on their own and are not roastable the same way. For detection, alert on Kerberos AS-REQ traffic with pre-authentication type 0 (Event ID 4768 with PreAuthType absent).

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1558.004: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, AS-REP Roasting
  • CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials
  • Microsoft: Kerberos pre-authentication

Name: Kerberoasting
Description:
# Description

One or more accounts have a Service Principal Name (SPN) registered in Active Directory. Any authenticated domain user, with no elevated rights, can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for those SPNs. The ticket is encrypted with the service account's password-derived key and cracks offline (hashcat mode 13100) to recover the cleartext password. The request is ordinary Kerberos traffic and produces no failed-logon on the target.

# Impact

The payoff is a service-account password, and service accounts are often the weak link: high-privilege identities (SQL, Exchange, SCCM, backup agents) set up years ago with a password that never changed. How bad it gets depends on that account's rights and on whether the password is weak enough to crack. A strong password holds; a weak one on a privileged account opens lateral movement and escalation. Cracking is offline, so only the initial TGS request is visible.

# Replication Steps
  • Request TGS tickets for every SPN-bearing account: GetUserSPNs.py {{DOMAIN}}/user:pass -dc-ip {{TARGET_HOST}} -request -outputfile kerb.hashes
  • Crack offline: hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hashes wordlist.txt

Service accounts confirmed roastable: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Move the SPN-bearing accounts above to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA), which use a 120-character password that rotates automatically. Where an SPN has to live on a normal user account, set a 25+ character random password and force AES-only ticket encryption (disable RC4 for the account) so the ticket is not worth cracking. For detection, watch for one account requesting many distinct service tickets in a short window (Event ID 4769), which is a strong roasting signal.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1558.003: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, Kerberoasting
  • CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials
  • Microsoft: Group Managed Service Accounts overview

Name: AD CS - Vulnerable Certificate Template or CA (ESC)
Description:
# Description

Active Directory Certificate Services has one or more misconfigurations in the ESC1 to ESC17 classes that allow certificate-based privilege escalation. Depending on the class, a low-privileged user can enroll for a certificate that authenticates as a higher-privileged principal, up to and including a Domain Controller (ESC8 via HTTP web enrollment and NTLM relay, or ESC1's enrollee-supplied SAN), without ever touching that principal's password.

# Impact

A successful abuse authenticates as a higher-privileged principal, and in the worst common cases that is a straight line to Domain Admin or Domain Controller. What makes it worse than a stolen password is persistence: a certificate stays valid until it expires and survives a password reset on the impersonated account, so it is a durable way back in. The real severity depends on which class is present and how privileged the reachable templates are.

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate vulnerable templates and CAs: certipy find -u user@{{DOMAIN}} -p pass -dc-ip {{TARGET_HOST}} -vulnerable -stdout
  • Abuse per class, e.g. ESC1: certipy req -u user@{{DOMAIN}} -template <tmpl> -upn administrator@{{DOMAIN}}

Vulnerable template(s) or CA(s) identified: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Fix per class: remove enrollee-supplied-SAN (CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT) from the templates above, require manager approval on sensitive templates, and cut enrollment and write rights down to the principals that actually need them. Disable HTTP Web Enrollment, or enforce Extended Protection for Authentication plus channel binding on it. Turn on strong certificate mapping (KB5014754) so an issued certificate cannot quietly impersonate an account through a weak UPN or SAN match.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1649: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
  • SpecterOps: Certified Pre-Owned (ESC1 to ESC8)
  • Microsoft KB5014754: Certificate-based authentication changes

Name: DCSync - Domain Credential Database Extraction
Description:
# Description

An account with directory-replication rights ran a DCSync (DRSUAPI replication) against a domain controller and pulled NTLM hashes out of the NTDS.dit database, which is the credential store for the whole domain. Holding and using Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All is Domain-Admin-equivalent, whatever groups the account is nominally in.

# Impact

This is full domain compromise. Every account's hash is available for pass-the-hash and offline cracking, and the krbtgt hash specifically lets an attacker forge Golden Tickets for domain persistence that outlives ordinary password resets. Once someone holds the credential database, there is nothing further in the domain to escalate to.

# Replication Steps
  • Replicate the credential database remotely: secretsdump.py {{DOMAIN}}/da:pass@{{TARGET_HOST}} -just-dc

Scope of extraction: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Treat the domain as compromised. Rotate all credentials, reset the krbtgt password twice (letting AD replication finish between resets), and rebuild trust from a known-good state rather than assuming one account cleanup covers it. Restrict Replicating Directory Changes and ...All to Domain Controllers only, and audit for any user or service account that currently holds them. For detection, alert on DRSUAPI replication sourced from a host that is not a DC (Event ID 4662 with the replication GUIDs, correlated to source IP).

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1003.006: OS Credential Dumping, DCSync
  • CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials
  • Microsoft: Reset the krbtgt account password

Name: SMB Signing Not Required
Description:
# Description

The host(s) at {{AFFECTED}} do not require SMB message signing. An attacker with a network position (via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning, a rogue DHCP or DNS answer, or a coercion primitive in the PetitPotam/PrinterBug family) can relay a captured or coerced authentication to these hosts and act as the coerced user, without ever recovering a password.

# Impact

A successful relay gives authenticated file-share access, remote command execution over SMB (PsExec-style), or local administrator on the relay target. If the relayed identity is privileged, or the target is a Domain Controller, the same weakness becomes a path to domain compromise. In practice this is usually the last link in a poisoning-to-domain-admin chain rather than a standalone problem, which is why it matters more in an AD environment than on an isolated host.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm signing is not required: nxc smb {{TARGET_HOST}} and look for signing:False
  • Relay a captured or coerced authentication: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support
Recommendation:
Enforce SMB signing everywhere through Group Policy (Microsoft network server/client: Digitally sign communications (always)), and confirm it on Domain Controllers, where current baselines enable it by default but it is still worth checking. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS (see the companion poisoning finding) to remove the most common way an attacker feeds this relay path. Signing stops the relay leg, not the credential capture, so both changes matter.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay
  • CWE-300: Channel Accessible by Non-Endpoint (Man-in-the-Middle)
  • Microsoft: Overview of Server Message Block signing

Name: SMB Null Session Allowed
Description:
# Description

The host(s) at {{AFFECTED}} allow anonymous (null) SMB sessions. An unauthenticated connection with an empty username and password (-u '' -p '') is accepted for RPC enumeration, which lets an attacker list local and domain users, groups, shares, and password policy without a single valid credential.

# Impact

This is reconnaissance, not direct access, but it feeds the attacks that follow. Enumerated usernames become the target list for password spraying and AS-REP/Kerberoast candidate selection, enumerated shares reveal more attack surface, and the disclosed password policy (lockout threshold, complexity) tells an attacker exactly how hard they can spray before tripping a lockout. On its own it is an information leak; its value is as a head start on everything else.

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate over the null session: enum4linux-ng -A {{TARGET_HOST}}
  • Confirm and pull users and shares directly: nxc smb {{TARGET_HOST}} -u '' -p '' --shares --users
Recommendation:
Restrict anonymous access: set RestrictAnonymous = 2 and RestrictAnonymousSAM = 1 (or the equivalent Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares Group Policy) across the domain. Remove shares that have no business reason to exist and tighten ACLs on the rest, so that even if a null session is ever re-enabled by mistake it discloses nothing useful.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1135: Network Share Discovery
  • CWE-287: Improper Authentication
  • CIS Microsoft Windows Benchmarks: anonymous access controls

Name: SMBv1 Enabled
Description:
# Description

The legacy SMBv1 dialect is enabled and negotiable on {{AFFECTED}}. SMBv1 is deprecated and has a history of serious remote-code-execution flaws, the best known being the MS17-010 (EternalBlue) class, CVE-2017-0144. Whether that specific risk applies here depends on patch level: the finding is that the old dialect is still offered, which is worth removing on its own.

# Impact

On a host that is unpatched for MS17-010, SMBv1 is a path to unauthenticated remote code execution as SYSTEM, and because the exploit needs no credentials and travels over SMB, it can spread to other SMBv1-reachable hosts. On a patched host the practical risk is smaller: SMBv1 lacks the protections of modern SMB and keeps a fragile legacy protocol in play. Confirm patch level before rating this any higher. An unpatched host moves it well up; a patched one keeps it a hardening issue.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm the dialect is offered: nxc smb {{TARGET_HOST}} and look for SMB1 in the supported dialects, or nmap --script smb-protocols -p445 {{TARGET_HOST}}
Recommendation:
Disable SMBv1 wherever legacy hardware or software does not explicitly require it (Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol, or the equivalent GPO), and confirm the host is patched for MS17-010 and later SMB CVEs regardless. Where a legacy dependency genuinely needs SMBv1, isolate that host on its own segment with no route to the rest of the environment.

References

  • Microsoft MS17-010 / CVE-2017-0144: SMBv1 remote code execution
  • CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
  • Microsoft: Stop using SMB1

Name: LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS Poisoning
Description:
# Description

Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR), NBT-NS, and/or mDNS are enabled on the local broadcast segment. When a host fails a normal DNS lookup (a mistyped share name, a stale mapped drive, a bad print or proxy lookup) it falls back to a broadcast query. An attacker on the same broadcast domain answers first, coerces the victim into authenticating to them, and captures its NetNTLMv2 challenge/response.

# Impact

The captured NetNTLMv2 hash can be cracked offline, or relayed straight to a host that does not require SMB signing (see the companion "SMB Signing Not Required" finding) for interactive access with no cracking at all. It is a low-effort move from a passive foothold on the wire to credentials or code execution, which is why it turns up so often in internal engagements. How far it goes depends on which accounts get captured and whether their hashes crack.

# Replication Steps
  • Capture passively: responder -I eth0 -wf, hashes arrive as victims resolve names that do not exist
  • Relay instead of cracking: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support

Credentials captured: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Disable LLMNR through Group Policy (Turn off multicast name resolution), disable NBT-NS per adapter or through the DHCP option pushed fleet-wide, and disable mDNS where nothing needs it. Enforce SMB and LDAP signing so a captured hash cannot simply be relayed even if some poisoning remains. Make sure DNS is configured correctly and completely so resolution never needs the broadcast fallback in the first place.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1557.001: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and Relay
  • CWE-300: Channel Accessible by Non-Endpoint (Man-in-the-Middle)

Name: Weak or Guessable Credentials
Description:
# Description

Credential testing (targeted brute force or password spraying) against in-scope network service(s) confirmed that one or more accounts accept a weak, default, or otherwise guessable password.

# Impact

This is direct authenticated access as the affected account. How far it goes depends on that account's rights and group memberships: a low-privilege user is a foothold, a privileged one is closer to game over. A single weak credential is often the one thing a well-hardened environment is missing, which is what makes it worth testing for.

# Replication Steps
  • Credential testing against the identified service(s) confirmed the account(s) below authenticate with the tested password: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Reset every affected credential to a strong, unique value, enforce a solid password policy (length over complexity, plus breached-password screening), and require MFA anywhere the service supports it. Remove or rotate default and installer accounts instead of leaving them at their shipped password. For detection, watch for spray patterns: many failed logons (Event ID 4625) across many accounts from one source in a short window, rather than repeated attempts against a single account.

References

  • MITRE ATT&CK T1110: Brute Force
  • CWE-521: Weak Password Requirements
  • NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines

Name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Description:
# Description

The application at {{TARGET_URL}} puts attacker-controlled input into a page without encoding it correctly for where it lands (HTML body, attribute, or script), so an attacker can run arbitrary JavaScript in a victim's browser under the site's own origin.

# Impact

In the browser, that means session hijacking, credential theft through a fake login overlay, forced actions as the victim, and phishing or defacement. The severity turns on the type: a reflected instance needs the victim to follow a crafted link and sits at the lower end, while a stored instance fires for every user who views the injected content, with no link to click, and belongs at the higher end.

# Replication Steps
  • Inject a probe such as <script>alert(document.domain)</script> (or a context-appropriate payload, e.g. an attribute breakout or event-handler payload where angle brackets are filtered) into the identified parameter and confirm it executes.

Location(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Apply context-aware output encoding to all untrusted data (HTML-entity encode in body context, JS-string encode inside <script>, attribute encode inside a tag attribute), and prefer a framework's auto-escaping templates over raw HTML sinks (innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html). Add a strict Content-Security-Policy as a backstop, and set HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite on session cookies so a successful injection still cannot read the session token directly.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A03:2021: Injection
  • OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

Name: SQL Injection
Description:
# Description

A parameter at {{TARGET_URL}} is concatenated straight into a SQL query instead of being bound as a parameter, so an attacker can change what the query does: add conditions, union in extra result sets, or chain statements through crafted input.

# Impact

The baseline is unauthorized read or modification of database contents, potentially every table the application's database account can reach, plus authentication bypass. Depending on the database engine, its configured privileges, and any file-system or command features left enabled, it can also reach remote code execution or lateral movement onto the database host. It is rated critical because the common case already exposes the data the application exists to protect, and the worst case is host compromise.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm with a boolean- or time-based probe (e.g. ' AND 1=1-- versus ' AND 1=2--, or ' OR SLEEP(5)--), then enumerate: sqlmap -u '{{TARGET_URL}}' --batch

Location(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Use parameterized queries or prepared statements (or a vetted ORM that does so by default) for every query that touches user input. String concatenation into SQL should not appear anywhere in the codebase. Run the application's database account with least privilege (no FILE or xp_cmdshell-class rights, no access beyond the schemas it needs), validate and allow-list input as a second layer, and treat a WAF rule as a stopgap, never the fix.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A03:2021: Injection
  • OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

Name: Exposed Version Control Directory (.git)
Description:
# Description

A version-control directory (.git/) is served at {{TARGET_URL}}, which exposes the repository's object database and commit history to anyone who asks. In practice that is read access to the application's source.

# Impact

An attacker can reconstruct the full source and its history and read it offline at their own pace, looking for more flaws. The history is the part people forget: credentials and API keys that were committed and later removed are still readable in earlier commits. How serious this is depends on what the repo holds. Live secrets in the history push it to the top of the range; an already-public codebase pulls it down.

# Replication Steps
  • Confirm exposure: request {{TARGET_URL}}/.git/HEAD and check for a valid ref response.
  • Reconstruct the repository: git-dumper {{TARGET_URL}}/.git/ ./dump

Location(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Block access to VCS metadata directories at the web server or reverse proxy (a deny rule for /.git/ and other dotfile directories), and better still, deploy from a build artifact that never includes .git so there is nothing to serve. Rotate any secret that appears anywhere in the exposed history, not just at the current tip: a credential removed in a later commit is still readable in an earlier one.

References

  • CWE-527: Exposure of Version-Control Repository to an Unauthorized Control Sphere
  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021: Security Misconfiguration

Name: Sensitive Information Disclosure
Description:
# Description

The application at {{TARGET_URL}} discloses sensitive information to unauthenticated users: verbose stack traces, internal file paths, software version banners, or a status/metrics endpoint (such as Apache server-status or an unauthenticated /metrics) that should not be reachable without authentication.

# Impact

Most of this is reconnaissance that speeds up a targeted attack: exact versions narrow the CVE search right away, internal paths and hostnames map the environment. Now and then the disclosed content is directly useful rather than just informative (a credential, a session token), which is what moves a given instance from low to something higher. Rate it on what is actually exposed.

# Replication Steps
  • Retrieve the disclosing endpoint(s) directly and review the response body for internals: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Turn off verbose and debug error output in production so a failure returns a generic message instead of a stack trace. Restrict or remove status, metrics, and diagnostic endpoints, or bind them to localhost and require authentication if they have to stay reachable. Suppress version banners on public-facing services, and review response bodies during code review for unintended exposure rather than leaning on a scanner to catch it.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021: Security Misconfiguration
  • CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

Name: Missing or Weak HTTP Security Headers
Description:
# Description

Responses from {{TARGET_URL}} omit or weakly configure defense-in-depth headers such as Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, and a frame-ancestors policy (or X-Frame-Options).

# Impact

On its own this is low risk. What it does is make other issues on the same origin easier to exploit and worse when they land: no CSP removes a backstop against XSS, no HSTS leaves a downgrade window on the first visit, no frame-ancestors policy allows clickjacking. Treat it as defense-in-depth to fix alongside the findings it would otherwise amplify, not as a standalone emergency.

# Replication Steps
  • Inspect response headers: curl -I {{TARGET_URL}}
Recommendation:
Add a Content-Security-Policy tailored to the application's real script and style sources (not a blanket unsafe-inline), Strict-Transport-Security with a long max-age and preload, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and a frame-ancestors CSP directive (or X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN for older browsers). Confirm the final header set with a headers scanner after deploying.

References

  • OWASP Secure Headers Project
  • CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure
  • MDN Web Docs: HTTP security headers

Name: Outdated or Vulnerable Software Component
Description:
# Description

A service or component reachable at {{AFFECTED}} is running an outdated version with known, published vulnerabilities, identified by banner or version fingerprinting and matched against public CVE records.

# Impact

This one has no single severity, because it depends on which CVE applies: an outdated component might carry a minor information leak or an unauthenticated remote code execution. What is consistent is that the weakness is public: the advisory names the affected versions and hands an attacker a starting point. A published advisory is not a ready exploit, though. Plenty of CVEs have no public exploit, and whether one lands depends on how the component is configured and reached. Rate the finding on the specific CVE(s) confirmed against this version, not on the fact that it is out of date, and confirm the version is actually reachable and exploitable before treating the worst listed CVE as the real risk.

# Replication Steps
  • Version identified through service or banner fingerprinting. Correlate the reported version against the vendor's advisories and the NVD for applicable CVEs.
Recommendation:
Patch or upgrade the affected component to a supported, fixed release. Check the specific CVE(s) for the exact fixed version, since a minor bump does not always include the fix. Put a recurring patch cadence in place rather than treating this as a one-time cleanup, and remove unused or end-of-life software instead of leaving it reachable.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A06:2021: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
  • CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
  • NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD)

Name: Exposed Administrative or Debug Endpoint
Description:
# Description

An administrative, management, or debug interface is reachable at {{TARGET_URL}} without adequate authentication or network restriction. It should require a login, or not be internet-reachable at all, and it does neither.

# Impact

What an attacker gets depends on the interface. Some only leak configuration; many admin and debug consoles ship an eval-style console or a file upload by design, which turns unauthenticated reach into configuration changes, credential access, or remote code execution, and from there full control of the application or its host. Rate it on what the specific interface exposes, and confirm whether authentication is truly absent or just weak.

# Replication Steps
  • Access the identified endpoint(s) directly and confirm no authentication is enforced: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Require strong authentication plus MFA on every management interface, and limit network reach to a trusted range or VPN rather than relying on the login alone. Strip debug endpoints and consoles out of production builds entirely, gated behind a build flag that cannot be flipped by an environment variable an attacker could influence.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021: Security Misconfiguration
  • CWE-749: Exposed Dangerous Method or Function

Name: Weak TLS/SSL Configuration
Description:
# Description

The service at {{AFFECTED}} negotiates weak TLS versions or cipher suites (SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1, RC4, export- or NULL-strength ciphers), presents an expired, self-signed, or hostname-mismatched certificate, or is otherwise open to a known TLS downgrade or attack class.

# Impact

This weakens the confidentiality and integrity of data in transit and gives a network-positioned attacker a chance at downgrade or man-in-the-middle interception. The severity scales with what actually crosses the connection: session tokens, credentials, or PII make it matter, a low-value public endpoint much less so. A real attack here also needs that network position, which is not always in reach.

# Replication Steps
  • Enumerate supported protocols, ciphers, and the certificate chain: sslscan {{TARGET_HOST}} or testssl.sh {{TARGET_HOST}}
Recommendation:
Disable SSLv3 and TLS 1.0/1.1 entirely, enable only TLS 1.2 and above with modern AEAD cipher suites (no RC4, no export or NULL ciphers), deploy a valid certificate from a trusted CA with the correct hostname(s), and enable HSTS once TLS is consistently correct. Use the Mozilla TLS "Intermediate" profile as a baseline, and re-scan afterward to confirm the weak options are actually gone rather than just deprioritized.

References

  • Mozilla Server Side TLS Guidelines
  • CWE-326: Inadequate Encryption Strength
  • NIST SP 800-52r2: TLS Guidelines

Name: Kubernetes Security Misconfiguration
Description:
# Description

Posture scanning of the Kubernetes cluster found control failures against recognized frameworks (NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance, MITRE ATT&CK for Containers): for example privileged or host-namespace workloads, missing default-deny NetworkPolicies, over-permissive RBAC bindings, or pods running without a restricted security context (root user, writable root filesystem, unneeded Linux capabilities kept).

# Impact

These weaken workload isolation and blast-radius control. Most are not exploited alone. The risk shows up in combination: a privileged pod plus over-permissive RBAC is a container-escape-to-cluster-admin chain, and a missing NetworkPolicy turns one compromised pod into free lateral movement across the namespace or cluster. Rate the set by the worst reachable combination, not by the raw count of failed controls.

# Replication Steps
  • Scan against the target kubeconfig: kubescape scan framework nsa,mitre --format json

Failing control(s): {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Fix the failing controls above: enforce Pod Security Standards at restricted, apply least-privilege RBAC (no wildcard verbs or resources, no cluster-admin bindings beyond genuine operators), default-deny NetworkPolicies with explicit per-workload allow rules, and non-root, read-only-root security contexts with capabilities dropped to what a workload actually needs. Re-run the same scan after remediation to confirm each control passes rather than assuming the change took.

References

  • NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance
  • MITRE ATT&CK for Containers
  • CIS Kubernetes Benchmark

Name: Exposed Network Service
Description:
# Description

Service fingerprinting found network service(s) on {{AFFECTED}} that may be unnecessary, unauthenticated, or reachable from a wider network segment than the service was meant to serve: commonly databases, management protocols, or legacy services that should be internal only.

# Impact

This widens the attack surface reachable from the tested position. An exposed service is not a vulnerability by itself, but an unauthenticated or weakly-authenticated one is among the fastest ways in, because it needs no phishing, no stolen credential, and no prior foothold, only network reach. Whether it matters here depends on what the service is and what it will accept from an unauthenticated caller.

# Replication Steps
  • Service(s) and banner(s) captured during fingerprinting: {{AFFECTED}}
Recommendation:
Restrict each exposed service above to the smallest network segment that needs it (firewalling and segmentation), require authentication on anything that has none, disable or remove services with no active business use, and put management protocols behind a bastion host or VPN instead of exposing them directly.

References

  • CIS Controls: Network Infrastructure Management
  • OWASP Top 10 A05:2021: Security Misconfiguration
